items.heading: You Get Into Event Management
items.text: You get into event management in India through one of two doors: structured education (a diploma, postgraduate diploma, or degree with real live-event training) or on-ground experience (an internship or entry-level coordinator role where you learn vendor coordination and logistics by doing them). Neither door is more legitimate than the other. What matters more than which door you use is picking a segment, weddings, corporate, exhibitions, concerts, or sports, deliberately, and building one piece of real proof before you apply anywhere.

items.heading: Job Postings and Course Brochures
items.text: Job postings and course brochures often talk about "event management" as one field. In practice, the client, the sales cycle, and the pressure points change completely depending on which of these five segments you end up working in.

items.heading: Strip Away the Segment Differences,
items.text: Strip away the segment differences, and most event management roles ask you to be reasonably good at five things at once, often on the same day.

items.heading: Budgeting
items.text: Budgeting: building a realistic cost sheet upfront, tracking spend against it, and knowing where to cut without the client noticing when something runs over.

items.heading: Logistics
items.text: Logistics: timelines, load-in and load-out schedules, permits, transport, and the dozens of small sequencing decisions that decide whether an event runs on time.

items.heading: Client Management
items.text: Client management: translating a vague brief into a workable plan, managing expectations honestly, and staying calm when a client changes their mind two days before the event.

items.heading: Budgeting
items.text: On-ground execution under pressure: the actual event day, where something will go wrong, a vendor is late, the weather shifts, a VIP guest changes plans, and someone has to make a fast decision without panicking.
